::: {.lead}
Almost every job now involves a screen. A game tester logs bugs in a shared
tracker, a designer presents ideas in slides, a marketer reads the analytics
of a social-media campaign, and a producer plans the work of a team in the
cloud. None of them is a programmer, yet all of them depend on digital
skills. This chapter defines what digital skills are, introduces the European
framework that describes them precisely, and explains why they decide
employability in today's labour market — and in the games industry in
particular.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary digital-skills digital-literacy digital-competence digcomp competence-area proficiency-level labour-market lifelong-learning >}}

## 1.1 Digital skills, digital literacy and digital competence

Three related terms are used in this course, from the narrowest to the
broadest.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 1.1 — Skills, literacy and competence"}
**Digital skills** are the practical abilities needed to use digital devices,
applications and networks — for example, to format a document, build a
spreadsheet formula or share a folder. **Digital literacy** adds
understanding and judgement: finding, evaluating, creating and communicating
information critically and safely. **Digital competence** is the broadest:
the confident, critical and responsible use of digital technology for
learning, work and participation in society, combining *knowledge*, *skills*
and *attitudes*.
:::

![Skills, literacy and competence: each contains the one before.](images/skills-circles.png){#fig-circles width=66%}

The difference matters. A student who can type quickly and knows every menu of
a word processor has good skills; a student who can also judge whether a
website is a reliable source, protect their account, respect the licence of an
image and choose the right tool for a task is digitally competent.

Digital skills are often described at three levels:

| Level | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| basic | using devices and common applications for everyday tasks | sending e-mail, searching, filling in an online form |
| intermediate (professional) | using specialised applications productively at work | analysing data in a spreadsheet, editing a promotional video |
| advanced (specialist) | creating and managing digital technology itself | programming a game, administering servers, securing networks |

: Levels of digital skills. {#tbl-levels}

Workers at the advanced level are called *ICT specialists*. Most jobs,
however, need the basic and intermediate levels across many tools rather than
deep specialisation in one — which is the subject of this course.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.1 — The digital skills of a game tester"}
A junior QA tester at a mobile-game studio spends one day as follows.

1. Signs in to the studio's systems with a password and a phone code
   (account security).
2. Installs the newest test build on three Android phones and an iPhone
   (using devices).
3. Plays the build, records a screen video of a bug and trims it (content
   creation).
4. Writes a clear bug report with steps, video and device data in a shared
   tracker (communication and collaboration).
5. Sorts the day's bugs in a spreadsheet by severity and device model
   (data analysis).

None of these tasks is programming, yet each one is a digital skill — and a
tester who lacks any of them slows down the whole team.
:::

## 1.2 The DigComp framework

To teach and assess digital competence consistently, the European Commission
publishes the **Digital Competence Framework for Citizens**, known as
**DigComp**. Its current version, DigComp 2.2 (2022), describes digital
competence in **five competence areas**, which contain **21 competences**
(@fig-digcomp).

![The five competence areas of DigComp 2.2 and their 21 competences.](images/digcomp-areas.png){#fig-digcomp width=96%}

| Area | Competences |
|---|---|
| 1 Information and data literacy | 1.1 browsing, searching and filtering data; 1.2 evaluating data and content; 1.3 managing data and content |
| 2 Communication and collaboration | 2.1 interacting; 2.2 sharing; 2.3 engaging in citizenship; 2.4 collaborating; 2.5 netiquette; 2.6 managing digital identity |
| 3 Digital content creation | 3.1 developing content; 3.2 integrating and re-elaborating content; 3.3 copyright and licences; 3.4 programming |
| 4 Safety | 4.1 protecting devices; 4.2 protecting personal data and privacy; 4.3 protecting health and well-being; 4.4 protecting the environment |
| 5 Problem solving | 5.1 solving technical problems; 5.2 identifying needs and technological responses; 5.3 creatively using digital technologies; 5.4 identifying digital competence gaps |

: The 21 competences of DigComp 2.2. {#tbl-digcomp}

### Proficiency levels

For each competence DigComp defines **eight proficiency levels**, grouped in
four bands (@fig-levels-ds). The levels differ in three ways: the
*complexity* of the tasks, the *autonomy* of the person (from needing
guidance to guiding others), and the *cognitive domain* (from remembering and
understanding to evaluating and creating).

![The eight DigComp proficiency levels in four bands.](images/proficiency.png){#fig-levels-ds width=84%}

| Band | Levels | A person at this band … |
|---|---|---|
| foundation | 1–2 | performs simple tasks, with guidance |
| intermediate | 3–4 | performs well-defined and routine tasks independently |
| advanced | 5–6 | performs different tasks and guides others |
| highly specialised | 7–8 | solves complex problems, proposes new ideas, leads |

: DigComp proficiency bands. {#tbl-bands}

The framework is not only a theory. Employers use its vocabulary in job
descriptions, schools and universities use it to design curricula, and the
European CV format, Europass, invites applicants to describe their digital
skills with its areas and levels. Free online self-assessment tools built on
DigComp ask a set of questions for each area and return a proficiency band,
which gives a learner a concrete starting point instead of a vague feeling of
being "good with computers".

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.2 — Placing tasks in DigComp"}
Classify four tasks from a game studio.

1. Checking whether a forum post about a new phone model is a reliable source
   before using its data: **1.2 evaluating data and content** (area 1).
2. Writing polite, clear messages in the team chat: **2.5 netiquette** (area 2).
3. Checking the licence of a free sound effect before putting it in a trailer:
   **3.3 copyright and licences** (area 3).
4. Noticing that one cannot yet build a PivotTable and taking an online course:
   **5.4 identifying digital competence gaps** (area 5).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Equating digital competence with programming. Programming is only *one* of
the 21 competences (3.4). A person can be highly competent in information,
communication, safety and problem solving without writing code — and a
programmer who ignores safety or copyright is not digitally competent.
:::

## 1.3 Digital skills and the labour market

The **labour market** is the meeting point between the skills that workers
offer and the skills that employers need. Three developments have moved
digital skills to its centre.

1. **Digitalisation of work.** Tasks in almost every sector — retail, health,
   media, logistics — are now carried out with digital tools. Job
   advertisements that ask for no digital skills at all have become rare.
2. **Automation.** Software and artificial intelligence take over routine
   tasks, while the demand grows for people who can use, check and combine
   these tools. Jobs change more often than they disappear: the tasks within
   them are redistributed between people and software.
3. **Policy targets.** Governments treat digital skills as infrastructure.
   The European Union's Digital Decade programme, for example, aims for at
   least 80 % of adults to have at least basic digital skills, and for 20
   million employed ICT specialists, by 2030 (@fig-targets).

![The EU Digital Decade targets for digital skills (2030).](images/eu-targets.png){#fig-targets width=80%}

Because tools change quickly, no degree can teach every application a
graduate will use. Employers therefore value two things above knowledge of a
particular program: the ability to learn new tools independently, and the
habit of doing so throughout one's working life — **lifelong learning**. The
DigComp competence 5.4, *identifying digital competence gaps*, describes
exactly this habit.

### Digital skills in the games industry

The games industry is an extreme case: it is entirely digital, its tools
change every year, and its teams are often distributed across countries.
@tbl-roles shows that every role, not only programming, relies on a specific
mix of digital competences — many of which this course teaches.

![Every role in a game studio depends on digital tools.](images/studio.png){#fig-studio width=92%}

| Role | Key digital tasks | DigComp areas | Course weeks |
|---|---|---|---|
| QA tester | bug reports, screen recordings, spreadsheets of results | 2, 3, 1 | 4, 6–7 |
| game designer | design documents, pitch presentations, data on player behaviour | 3, 1 | 4–5, 9 |
| producer | cloud planning, shared documents, budgets, reports | 2, 1 | 2, 6, 9 |
| community and marketing manager | social media, landing pages, analytics | 2, 3, 1 | 12–14 |
| data analyst | databases, spreadsheets, dashboards | 1, 5 | 6–11 |
| everyone | secure accounts, privacy, licences, netiquette | 4, 3, 2 | 3, 13 |

: Digital competences in game-industry roles. {#tbl-roles}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 1.3 — Reading a job advertisement"}
A studio advertises a "Junior Community Manager". The requirements include:
*"manage our Discord and social channels; prepare weekly reports of
engagement in spreadsheets; create simple graphics and short videos; build
event pages; handle player data responsibly."*

1. Managing channels and engaging players: area 2 (communication and
   collaboration).
2. Weekly spreadsheet reports: area 1 (managing and evaluating data).
3. Graphics, videos and event pages: area 3 (digital content creation).
4. Responsible handling of player data: area 4 (safety — personal data and
   privacy).
5. A candidate can use this mapping to find their own gaps (area 5) before
   applying.
:::

## Case study: Pixel Harbor Studio

*Pixel Harbor* is a small mobile-game studio with eight employees working
partly from home. It is hiring two juniors — a QA tester and a marketing
assistant — and asks every candidate to describe their digital skills using
the DigComp areas and levels. The exercises below and the Game challenge of
the interactive lesson use this studio.

The interactive lesson contains a **DigComp self-check**: rate yourself on the
21 competences and see your profile by area. Scan the code to open it.

## Exercises

1. Explain the difference between digital skills and digital competence, with
   an example of a person who has the first but not the second.
2. Name the five DigComp areas.
3. To which competence does each task belong: (a) installing the
   security updates of a phone; (b) using a reference manager to organise sources; (c) adjusting
   screen time to avoid eye strain; (d) writing a simple script; (e) choosing
   a video tool for a new task?
4. How many competences does DigComp 2.2 contain, and how many proficiency
   levels does each competence have?
5. Describe the three dimensions in which the proficiency levels differ.
6. A student can follow instructions to share a file but cannot do it alone.
   Which band of proficiency is this?
7. Give two reasons why automation increases, rather than decreases, the
   importance of digital skills.
8. State two targets of the EU Digital Decade for digital skills.
9. Choose one role in @tbl-roles and list three digital tasks it requires,
   each with its DigComp area.
10. *Pixel Harbor*: write a three-line description of your own digital
    skills for the QA tester position, naming one area and one level in each
    line.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Skills are practical abilities (e.g. fast typing, knowing menus); competence adds knowledge, judgement and attitudes (e.g. evaluating sources, protecting data). A fast typist who shares passwords has skills without competence.
2. Information and data literacy; communication and collaboration; digital content creation; safety; problem solving.
3. (a) 4.1 protecting devices; (b) 1.3 managing data and content; (c) 4.3 protecting health and well-being; (d) 3.4 programming; (e) 5.2 identifying needs and technological responses.
4. 21 competences; 8 levels each.
5. Complexity of tasks, autonomy, cognitive domain.
6. Foundation (levels 1–2).
7. Routine tasks move to software, so workers must use, check and combine digital tools; tools change, so workers must keep learning.
8. At least 80 % of adults with basic digital skills; 20 million employed ICT specialists (by 2030).
9. For example, producer: shared planning documents (2), budgets in spreadsheets (1), reports (3).
10. Individual answer; each line names an area and a level, e.g. "Safety — intermediate: I use a password manager and two-factor authentication on all accounts."
:::
